Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Tamworth District Court
Marius St & Fitzroy Street,
Tamworth NSW 2340
Tuesday, 17 September 2024 at 10am
(Day 50)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney SC with Mr Hernan Pinto-Lopez
for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning, everyone. Just before
I take appearances and hear anything by way of opening
statements, because this is the first day of the hearings
here in Tamworth for this inquiry, I'd like to acknowledge
that we meet today on the traditional lands of the Gomeroi
people. I recognise their continuing connection to this
land and pay my respects to Elders past and present, and
I extend that respect to any Aboriginal people present
today or who might be listing or watching online.
Mr Glover.
MR GLOVER: Commissioner, I appear with my learned friend
Mr Fuller for this hearing block.
MR CHENEY: Commissioner, with your leave I appear with Mr
Pintos-Lopez for NSW Health.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thank you, Mr Cheney.
MR GLOVER: Commissioner, the hearing block this week
commences the last of our regional hearings. By the end of
the week, we will have sat in Wagga, Wagga, Dubbo, Broken
Hill, Batemans Bay and now Tamworth. Save for Albury, this
week also concludes our visits to the regional parts of
New South Wales.
Throughout the work of the inquiry we have now
visited each rural and regional LHD, met with and heard
from many people: clinicians, health administrators, and
members of the public. Although much of the focus of the
work of this inquiry has necessarily been on the
identification of issues and challenges facing the delivery
of healthcare in New South Wales, what has remained
constant throughout our travels, including over the last
few weeks, is the dedication of those working within the
healthcare sector, within NSW Health and outside of it, to
caring for their patients and communities across the State.
This week also is the culmination of the inquiry's
visits to the northeast part of New South Wales, visiting
the northern New South Wales LHD, the Mid North Coast LHD
and now Hunter New England. We began our travels a couple
of weeks ago now in the Northern NSW LHD, visiting Lismore,
Ballina and Tweed Heads. Whilst in Lismore, we visited the
Lismore Base Hospital and met with clinicians and
management in a round table setting. As always, and

I might say this a few times in this brief opening this
morning, those discussions with incredibly valuable in
understanding the challenges faced by those on the ground
in the region but also some of the successes they've had in
the face of adversity.
On that note, we heard from those involved in
delivering care through the devastating floods that
impacted Lismore in 2022. For those of us who watched from
afar during that period, it is somewhat difficult to
comprehend the devastation that affected that community,
but what we heard were some incredible stories of
resilience and commitment by those in that region. For
example, we heard of staff who, despite having lost their
own homes to those floods, attended the hospital for their
shift no less than 48 hours later. We also heard of some
ingenuity in people getting medical services to where they
were needed, including transporting some rather high tech
medical equipment in taxis to ensure it got where it needed
to be.
Whilst in Lismore, we also had the benefit of meeting
with the local Aboriginal community Controlled Health
Organisation, Rekindling the Spirit, and with the drug and
alcohol service, Namatjira Haven. Engaging with those
involved in delivering care to Indigenous communities in
the regions has been a valuable part of the work of the
inquiry, and the opportunities to do so in Lismore and in
the other places we visited was no exception.
We have also heard evidence throughout the inquiry of
the benefits of training being undertaken in rural and
regional areas and we were fortunate to visit the
University Centre for Rural Health in Lismore. There, we
heard again the benefits of students spending more time in
rural and regional areas during their undergraduate,
training but also of the benefits of students across
disciplines training and living together, with a view to
fostering the type of integrated care approach and
understanding between those in different disciplines of the
work that they each do.
In Ballina, we met with the PHN that covers the vast
district of the northern New South Wales LHD and the Mid
North Coast LHD, Healthy North Coast. There, we heard of
the benefits of joint planning and commissioning across the
primary and acute care sectors and what might be done to

improve that to lead to better delivery of services. We
also saw what might be the future of an integrated primary
care practice at First Light Healthcare.
In Tweed Heads, we met with the Bulgarr Ngaru Medical
Corporation and heard about their initiatives to
deliver better healthcare to the Indigenous communities of
that region, and their views on how services might be
better integrated between those of services like theirs and
those offered by NSW Health.
From there, we travelled north to the newly opened
Tweed Valley Hospital. That facility was opened only
in May of 2024. Whilst there, we had the fortune of being
introduced to the site by Cameron, a local Indigenous
artist, who explained to us the significance of the site on
which the hospital is built to the Indigenous community,
but also how art has been integrated into the build to make
it a more welcoming and safe experience for those
First Nations communities. The round table at Tweed Valley
Hospital was again very worthwhile.
At times, we have heard evidence during this inquiry
of the disparity in award conditions between
New South Wales and neighbouring states. The disparity is
in sharp focus in the northern parts of the State with the
lure of Queensland, and we heard from some clinicians in
the very early stages of their careers about the very real
decisions they have to make as to whether they stay south
of the border in New South Wales or whether they take the
short trip north to better conditions, and I expect you
will hear some evidence about that over the next few days.
The next stop in our visit was the Mid North Coast
LHD, beginning in Coffs Harbour. Whilst in the regions, we
again had a number of beneficial meetings with local
clinicians and Aboriginal medical services, and I think it
is fair to say that there was a general consensus across
each of those meetings that there is a need for enhanced
coordination and joint planning of services between those
in the primary care and the Indigenous care space and those
in the acute care sectors.
Whilst in Coffs Harbour, we visited the Coffs Harbour
Health Campus. There, we saw some of that facility and met
with more clinicians and managers. We heard of the
challenges in recruiting and retaining staff and, indeed,

the lure of Queensland from that far south in the State.
We also heard firsthand of the effects on the hospital
services of the lack of aged care facilities and NDIS
facilities, leading to a large number of patients remaining
in hospital when they are ready for discharge. Not only is
that a bad outcome for those patients, but we had some
demonstration of the knock-on effects that that may have to
hospital services, including in surgery lists and in the
emergency department.
We then visited the Bowraville HealthOne facility.
That is a service that includes general practice and is one
that is operated by the LHD. You will hear a little bit
more about that initiative, but it is an example of the LHD
stepping in to provide primary care where there was no
market. As might be expected, we are told that the initial
evaluations of that service have led to greatly increased
health outcomes, but also flow-on effects to the delivery
of other services in the LHD.
From there, we travelled to Port Macquarie and Port
Macquarie Base Hospital. That round table involved some
thought-provoking discussions about what the public health
system might look like, echoing some of the comments that
were made by Commissioner Garling in his inquiry about the
need to have a discussion about how one designs the public
health service to ensures its sustainability going forward.
Yesterday, whilst in Tamworth we visited the Tamworth
Hospital and we had two round tables: one concerning the
delivery of maternity and obstetric services and another
focusing on the challenges like we heard in Mid North Coast
around patient length of stay.
We were also fortunate to receive a presentation on
some innovative steps taken in the district around
sustainability in housing, and we heard that those
initiatives have already delivered significant benefits,
both environmentally and financially, to the district.
Members of the inquiry team also met with the Tamworth
Aboriginal Medical Service and we were hosted by the
University of Newcastle's regional training hub. Similar
to the benefits of rural training that we heard and saw
first-hand in Lismore, we again heard about the benefits of
long-term exposure to students across the disciplines, both
medical, nursing and allied health, to training and

placements in rural and regional areas.
In this block of hearings, Commissioner, you will hear
some evidence that is drawn from each of the LHDs that we
visited over the last few weeks, and in addition to those
witnesses that are to be called, there are a number of
statements that will be tendered, although you won't hear
directly from those witnesses this week.
With that short opening, the first witness to be
called is Dr David Scott, and Mr Fuller will take that
witness.
THE COMMISSIONER: You don't want to say anything,
Mr Cheney?
MR CHENEY: No, your Honour.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes, Dr Scott. I am not actually sure
where the witness box is. It's over there, is it? Very
good.
<DAVID ROBERT SCOTT, AFFIRMED [10.12 am]
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Fuller.
<EXAMINATION BY MR FULLER
MR FULLER: Q. Thank you, Commissioner. Dr Scott, would
you state your full name please?
A. David Robert Scott.
Q. Your professional address is Dean Street, Tamworth,
New South Wales, 4340; is that right?
A. That's right.
Q. You are a physician and gastroenterologist VMO at
Tamworth Rural Referral Hospital; that's right?
A. That's right.
Q. And you are also chair of the Tamworth Hospital
Medical Staff Council; that's right?
A. That's right.
Q. You've prepared a statement to assist the inquiry?
A. I have.

Q. I'll ask you just be given a hard copy of that to make
it easier for you, but the document number is
[MOH.0011.0055.0001] and it is proposed to be exhibit K-41
in the tender bundle, Commissioner.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR FULLER: Q. Dr Scott, you have a got a copy of your
statement. Have you had the opportunity to review your
statement recently?
A. I have.
Q. Is everything in it true and correct to the best of
your knowledge?
A. It is, yep.
Q. Thank you. That will be tendered in due course,
Commissioner.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR FULLER: Q. Dr Scott, you have worked as a VMO at
Tamworth Hospital since 2010; is that right?
A. That's right.
Q. What's the nature of your VMO appointment? Is it a
sessional appointment or a fee-for-service appointment? Do
you know what I mean?
A. Both. So ward rounds and clinics are sessional, and
then - but I do procedures as a gastroenterologist and they
are fee-for-service.
Q. What proportion of your time do you spend working at
Tamworth Hospital in comparison with your other work that
you have told us about in your statement?
A. It'd be two-fifths of the week, probably.
Q. You told us you also work at Tamara Private Hospital?
A. Yeah.
Q. That's right? Is that also in Tamworth?
A. That is. Just down the road.
Q. And you also work at Gunnedah Hospital; is that right?
A. Once every two months.
Q. Can I ask you, please, to have a look at paragraph 7

of your statement. You've told us there - thank you, it is
just coming up electronically as well. You told us in that
paragraph about decreasing numbers of GPs in rural and
regional facilities and privately, that's in the first
sentence. Are you able to quantify in any way the decrease
that you're referring to?
A. Well, I guess there is a distinction between decrease
in GPs in the town and decrease in GPs at the hospital.
When I first came to Tamworth, Gunnedah would have had,
I would have thought, six to eight GPs who had practices in
the town and would admit patients to the hospital and that
number I think would be less than that now, quite a bit
less, I'd imagine. I know, for example, like, at Inverell
it is not uncommon we get calls from the emergency
department there with patients that might need a brief
admission but there is no-one who can admit the patient to
the hospital because a doctor in emergency can't admit and
vice versa, so there is a distinction between those who
work in the town and those who work at the hospital.
Q. Starting with the hospital in at least Gunnedah and
Inverell, you have observed a decrease in the number of GPs
since your time --
A. Working at the hospital, absolutely. Absolutely.
Q. And what about privately, which is the other part of
what you referred to?
A. Look, harder to judge, because a lot more GPs come as
registrars or they come for a brief time. So a lot of
names come across, but I am never quite sure who is still
there and who is not, so I probably couldn't give an exact
answer. I suspect it would be less overall. That's what
people tell me, but I couldn't give you a number on that.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Is - I mean, you don't have the
precise data but having long experience in the medical
system, you'd get anecdotal sort of comments made to you
about whether GP numbers in private practice are decreasing
and that's the sense you get from that feedback?
A. I know more than - a number of patients from Gunnedah
now have GPs in Tamworth because they couldn't get one
locally, and I met one recently who has got a GP in Sydney
because that just was actually more convenient. They're
near where their daughter lives. They're having to travel
a lot further to find a private GP.
Q. In relation to these Gunnedah patients you are talking

about, is it the case that they can't get a GP at all in
Gunnedah or they can't see one in a timely manner? Or
both?
A. Possibly both, but at least some have told me they
can't - the books are closed, so to speak.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes, okay.
MR FULLER: Q. You've referred in paragraph 7 - tell me
if I've got this right - to those, the issues you've
described, creating pressure on the ED at Tamworth
Hospital. Is that a correct understanding of what you are
saying?
A. That's right.
Q. Can you just describe how that actually plays out in
practice, based on your observations?
A. So maybe a few different ways. The lack of GPs in
general who could have dealt with some urgent but minor
issues mean that those patients might end up at the
emergency department, and patients may choose to come to
Tamworth emergency department for the lack of just general
practice. Secondly, the Gunnedah Hospital, for example,
but a lot of hospitals like that, have troubles getting GPs
or doctors to be there on-site, and so the patients may be
able to present the emergency department but then get sent
to Tamworth because there is no doctor there who can deal
with the particular issue. Or even if they meet a
telehealth doctor in those local - those smaller hospitals,
they might still feel a patient needs to go to Tamworth
Hospital. And then beyond that, not just having doctors in
town, in the hospital, but also the doctors with the right
skills. So that some of the doctors who work in these
towns have extraordinarily broad skills, procedural skills,
which can deal with a lot of issues in situ, but as the
skill level drops of the average doctor in those emergency
departments, the need to transfer to a bigger centre
increases, and so that also flows into Tamworth Hospital.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. What are the consequences for
your practice as a physician to both the care you provide,
but also for your patients if that patient doesn't have
ready access to a GP?
A. As an outpatient?
Q. Yes.
A. Oh, there's a lot. So other than the presentations to

hospital to deal with these short-term issues, just
long-term preventative healthcare automatically takes a
second place behind dealing with the acute problem.
I can't discharge patients from my care to make room for
more because I've got to keep seeing them to deal with
these sort of long-term things which are not - which a GP
could do very comfortably. And just the need to hang on to
people in hospital as well, just a few extra days, just
because - with this situation everything is really set
before they go, rather than the thing's mostly right, "See
your GP next week and just make sure."
Q. You don't have that security?
A. That's right.
Q. Primary care VMO.
A. Yeah, yeah. So just it puts more burden on the
hospital and on the specialist to just hang onto them a bit
longer. And obviously the patient. Amongst others, has a
more difficult process as well, especially if they are from
outside town.
MR FULLER: Q. Do you perceive those issues as being a
significant or substantial problem for Tamworth Hospital?
A. Yes. Yes.
Q. You have told us at the end of paragraph 7 of your
statement about the introduction of urgent care clinics in
your area. Firstly, where have those been introduced in
the area that affects your work?
A. So I am only aware of one. It started in Tamworth.
I'm not quite sure of the exact model, but the idea is it
is a walk-in-type system. And I gather they've been
quite - the uptake has been quite good in the sense they
have been seeing lots of patients. When I asked my
emergency department colleagues whether they felt a
perceptible difference from that urgent care clinic
starting, they haven't felt that. Now, the numbers may
not - the numbers may show there has been a decline, but
I guess they are working at a capacity all the time and one
wouldn't feel that difference. But as a model, it seems
like a good thing to do.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. This isn't necessarily a question
for Dr Scott, but is this urgent care clinic in Tamworth,
is it one of the Commonwealth ones or is it a State service
one? You don't know?

A. I wouldn't know, no.
THE COMMISSIONER: "Clinic" usually, I think, is, what,
for the Commonwealth? Yes.
MR FULLER: Q. In terms of your own practice and
delivery of services to your patients, has the urgent care
clinic impacted on that in any way?
A. Not that I've noticed.
Q. In paragraph 8 - and I think you mentioned this
earlier - you told us about fewer rural GPs having extended
scope of practice than they used to - do you have any
observations as to why that change has happened?
A. So all of the factors that people find would deter
them from a career in rural general practice would apply,
but in particular it is harder to take on these more
advanced skills where the gain might be higher but the risk
is also very high. And you might be doing some of these
procedures occasionally, you know, in the middle of the
night when things are tough, versus some specialist
colleagues do them in a hospital setting, daylight hours,
but you are nevertheless compared against what you can
provide compared to that. So the risk is quite high in
providing that service. There are ways to get trained in
it if you make the effort, but the risk in providing it is
quite high and I can see why people don't. It would seem -
it doesn't make sense that the reward for that sort of
service is equivalent and the standard is equivalent when
you try and provide that service as well.
Q. Just in terms of the risk, do you perceive that as
having increased over time? And if not, what's the reason
why it has caused a reduction for rural GPs?
A. I mean, I guess perception, yes, it has increased.
I think community expectations are higher now. I think the
community wants, and it is entitled to want, a high-level
service delivered in their home town, and sort of the "near
enough is a good enough" approach that the local doctor
might have provided, you know, if it ever was acceptable,
it isn't now. And there's more standardisation of
technique, and so unless you are really on top of all
those, you know, developments and changes to protocols,
which is hard when you are only doing one of these every so
often, the chance that you have done something which wasn't
considered standard of care would be higher.

Q. At the end of paragraph 8, you've said that payment
structures may need to change to reward people with
extended skills in areas of need. Is that what you were
referring to just before about the idea of providing an
incentive for people to develop these skills in rural
areas?
A. I think so. You can't expect - if you are paying
someone the same to do a job which is difficult and they
don't do often and in a complex situation, paying the same
as a person who does it all the time every day, where in
fact - especially if it gets more than the GP does
sometimes for some procedures, it just doesn't make sense
if you're going to - people are going to want to take those
skills to these towns.
Q. Do you have any other views based on your observations
and experience about changes that could be made to improve
the - increase the attractiveness of that kind of work in
developing that skillset in rural general practice?
A. Well, incentives are more than just financial. The
reward needs to be flexible enough that they're not bound
by the same, you know, obligations, and there can be some -
not just financial but in terms of conditions, in terms of
facilities, you know, opportunities for more training,
equipment that they might want. That all needs to be part
of a package, to say if you come to a town, provide these
sort of services, we want to encourage you and support you
to do that, rather than slapping the same award in front of
them and saying, "This is all there is."
Q. Do you have any particular kinds of conditions in mind
that you think might help if they were more flexible?
A. Well, maybe - yeah, beyond what I just said, probably
not. Just, yeah, opportunities for more education and
equipment as well. Sometimes it's easy to get the time off
to go to a conference and you come home with all these
great ideas but you can't buy the kit to do it, so that
needs to be part of it as well.
Q. Do you think, particularly for more junior
practitioners, having some sort of support from more senior
practitioners, whether in person every so often or
remotely, might assist?
A. Probably. Probably. That's always handy, but in
practice, often these things have to be done at the time
and there's usually not a lot of time to sort of chat about
it.

Q. Do you, based on your experience in a small hospital,
do you perceive on-call as being a particular issue for
practitioners who might work in those hospitals?
A. Oh, absolutely. Yep. Yep.
Q. And so that might be a kind of commission that could
be looked at if someone were to receive a higher payment
for working on-call?
A. Yeah. The sort of doctor that works in the country in
general and, in particular these towns, is - they are
normally very committed. They're clinicians. They like
seeing sick people and trying to make them better. And so
sometimes the on-call is not the burden, it is part of why
they do what they do. So I wouldn't want to be simplistic
and say they all want less on-call, but there needs to be a
sense when they walk in, doing the on-call, that the system
is going to facilitate what they want, what they're trying
to do.
Q. So to your mind it's perhaps more about, or at least
as much about having adequate supports in place for these
doctors as it is about pay, for example?
A. Yes. So pay is part of it, people as they are, but
it's more than that, yes.
Q. In paragraph 9 of your statement, you talk about
virtual services like My Emergency Doctor. You told us you
think they may be an effective temporary solution but not
an effective replacement of clinical staff. Can you just
elaborate on your views about that?
A. Look, so I certainly understand why it's come about in
the sense that there is a lot of smaller hospitals who
can't run a 24-hour roster with the local staff, and so
these either fill gaps or can replace an entire section of
the care. So I can understand that, and obviously we can't
just turn it off overnight. But the stories you get from
the patients and the staff that are in those facilities, it
is certainly far short of having the doctor there. So one
of the nurses in Gunnedah mentioned - I think I put some of
it in here - that she might have a child - the only nurse
in Gunnedah emergency overnight, no doctor, so a child
comes in with a sore ear or whatever. She has to then sit
in the consultation with the My Emergency Doctor, who takes
the whole story again, gets her to examine the patient sort
of in front of them on the computer, then he has a
discussion and then there is a prescription maybe and, you

know, all the time she has also got other patients out
there that are needing help and with a doctor on site,
she'd say, "You look after this one, I'll look after this
one." Also then there's a, sitting in the sort of Tamworth
Hospital, our view is a bit distorted, but it sounds like
that these doctors, they don't understand the local
strengths and weaknesses. They don't say, "Well if we can
just get them over till tomorrow morning, so-and-so will
come on call tomorrow morning," or, "Tomorrow morning the
scanner will be open and if we can do - deal with the
problem there." They don't understand sort of the local
vagaries or, "This guy is on holidays so there is no
someone - there is no-one there on Monday morning. You've
got to send this patient out." Like, those subtleties are
lost, which local people would be all over. And so, more
often than maybe needs to be, the patients end up flowing
to Tamworth where they wouldn't have had to otherwise.
Then of course you have got all the training of the staff.
I mean, these doctors aren't involved in teaching or
training. They are just there to see the patient, they
move on. There is no sense of buy-in to the community or
to the hospital in general. They are not going to
contribute to advocating for better conditions or equipment
or whatever. They are not the equivalent in all those
other ways. They are not going to teach medical students.
They are so far short. So from a patient's point of view
they're short and from a hospital's point of view they're
well short of the local doctor.
Q. Do you see a long-term place for virtual care in rural
and regional locations at all, and if so, what is it?
A. Look, I guess I do. From the trends. Not because
I think it's the best model of care, but just the way
workforces patterns are developing. I don't think it has
to be like that, but it seems to be the way. If I had some
choice, I'd probably disincentivise that model of care. I
think if you have just trained as an emergency physician,
you've got a - you know, you are living in Sydney or
somewhere, you know, there are all these jobs around the
countryside you can go and do, or you can just sit in
Sydney and do them all, you know, whenever you want to.
There is little incentive to come. If My ED Doctor didn't
exist or at least wasn't so widely used, you'd say, "Well,
I have got to feed my kids. I better go get one of these
jobs." So disincentivising people to do these virtual
things as part of a solution does sort of feed on itself in
some ways.

Q. Would it be fair to say that your view is that it
would be better use of resources to invest in incentivising
people to actually go and live and work in these rural
communities rather than virtual care in your view?
A. Yeah. I don't pretend it to be cheaper, but it would
be better.
Q. In paragraph 10 and following, you tell us your views
about the centralisation and decentralisation of services
in Hunter New England LHD. Firstly, can I - by its
services and equipment. Can I just ask you to summarise
the kinds of services and equipment that you have in mind
when you're talking about - let me ask that in a different
way.
You talked about services and equipment being
centralised at John Hunter Hospital. What sort of services
and equipment are you concerned about having been
centralised?
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. You've given the example of
pacemaker insertion as one example you have given.
A. Yeah. So it's more - so, ultimately, there will have
to be some centralisation of some, you know, more complex
procedures and therapy. You know, that's fine. But we
concede that ground easily. So pacemaker insertion has
been happening in Newcastle for a long time. We had a
cardiologist who moved to town a few years ago, who was up
to date with all those skills, wanted to bring it here, but
it seemed like such a big effort to bring it in. And when
it already exists in Newcastle, there seems no reason - the
doctors there are no more qualified than here. There seems
no reason why it couldn't happen here. Faecal
transplantation, a similar thing. The process already
exists in Newcastle, but bringing it here was a big
palaver. You know?
Q. Sticking with pacemaker insertion, what should I take
from that, that there is an absence of a cath lab here and
there could be one??
A. No, we have a cath lab here. But once again picking
on - well, picking on cardiology, there are fewer
cardiologists in Tamworth compared to any equivalent-sized
town in the State. There is fewer - there is less cath lab
access in this town compared to the other cath labs in
equivalent-sized hospitals in the State. And there seems

no good reason for that. We have the demand. Certainly we
have the people who want and are able to do the work.
Q. So "demand" means you've got people in Tamworth and
surrounds have cardiovascular disease at the same rates?
A. A couple of them, yeah. Well, no, higher rates.
Q. Higher rates?
A. Than those living in Newcastle and Sydney. Higher
rates.
Q. And you think there wouldn't be a trouble in finding
the right physicians to --
A. So we have a --
Q. -- provide those services?
A. We have a doctor at the moment in Tamworth who is
working sort of as a sort of fellowship role. He is
trained, but obviously working with a fellowship role. He
would like to stay here with his wife, who is also a
doctor, live in Tamworth, work as a cardiologist here. It
